r7-m01.abandon: The board already contradicts the mechanism. The mechanism says that when the cued base misses a problem it solves in its other samples, the wrong sample started on a working line of attack, wrote a switch phrase, and ended on a later wrong line. It also says RL's gain comes from switching less. (1) result-afc423 judged exactly those samples: "Base items with a right sibling: 39 of 48 slip/misread/format". Wrong plan, the only label a switch to a wrong line would produce, is the minority, and it is concentrated where the base never succeeds: "without (base 0/4): 8 of 12 wrong plan". The error also comes early, not after a first attempt: "First wrong step at median 0.20 of the answer." (2) knowledge-1a0674 finds no abandoned right first attempt: "the cued base overwrites a right first answer: 0 of its v3-wrong MATH-500 answers have a right first marker." (3) result-faf15a finds that RL's advantage is not in the choice of line: "RL lowers misreadings and slips, not wrong plans." It gives the per-label numbers "By label for Math 3.1: misread -1.52, slip -0.72, wrong plan +0.03", so RL does not avoid the wrong-plan steps the mechanism says switching causes. (4) result-5e17a6 hand-labelled the 65 RL-only problems: only "2 reached gold then changed it" (plus 9 wrong method and 2 drift), against 14 misread, 14 arithmetic/algebra slip and 16 cap hits. Taken together, the base's misses on problems it can solve are within-line slips and misreadings that RL lowers. They are not working lines abandoned after a switch phrase, so a switch-token penalty has no failure mode to act on.

r7-m02.abandon: The mechanism says T 0.6's better finished-answer accuracy comes from removing tail draws at early plan decisions (forks), so cooling only the first ~1,000 tokens should keep that gain without loops. Two board items already contradict the cause it names. (1) result-34897a cooled exactly the fork positions over the whole answer and got no finished-answer gain: 'T 1.0 with T 0.6 where entropy > 0.9 nats (mean of 2 samples 403.5)' with 'Cap hits per 500: T 1.0 22.5, forks only 33, confident only 44, both (T 0.6) 98'. That is 403.5 right of 467 finished (86.4 %) against plain T 1.0's 410.5 of 477.5 (86.0 %). The ten extra cap hits should, if anything, have raised that ratio by selection. Cooling confident positions instead gives 403.5 of 456 (88.5 %). So what rise there is in finished accuracy follows cooling at confident (slip) positions, not at forks where plans are chosen. An early-only window covers a subset of those same forks, so it cannot recover a gain that cooling all forks did not produce. (2) result-faf15a finds that the base's located wrong steps are more probable than their own control text, not tail draws: 'Under the base the wrong step has log-prob -0.53 per token vs -0.63 for control text (W4 refuted): truncation or low temperature cannot remove these steps'. For wrong plans in particular RL does not lower them either ('wrong plan +0.03'). The '94 % vs about 90 %' contrast the mechanism starts from (knowledge-13cff3: 'on the 402 problems that finish at T 0.6, T 1.0 gets 361-364 against 378') conditions on the T 0.6 sample itself finishing. A wrong T 0.6 line tends to loop and drop out, so the contrast is at least partly selection, not evidence of better early decisions. That is the reading items (1) and (2) support.

The second half holds the steps farthest from the statement. There, given a sound prefix, the base finishes as well as RL: 'Right prefixes from 50 % on: both finish equally (83 vs 83 of 88 base prefixes; 131 vs 134 of 140 RL prefixes)'. On wrong prefixes the edge also disappears at the latest cut: '+5.7 [-2.9, 14.3] at 75 %'. The same item reports 'Refuted: 'late checking' (no RL edge at 75 %)'. Under m04 the base's recall is weakest in that region, so RL's edge should be largest there. It is zero. m04's holds_against answers result-a6ab7a only by saying distance can grow inside the first half. That does not explain why the edge is absent at the largest distances. (2) The errors sit near the statement, not far from it. result-afc423 reports 'First wrong step at median 0.20 of the answer'. result-faf15a locates the steps at a 'median 29 tokens' long, and result-5e17a6 finds the base's short answers mostly right ('Base answers <= 2,000 tokens: 263, 13 wrong'). (3) In-context reading does not separate the models where it was tested. result-c4411d: 'RL does not read partial results better (chains -0.007 [-0.04,0.03])'. result-abb853: 'every standard set equal' on the workspace and multihop tests. A restatement prefilled right after the cue sits about 100 tokens from the original statement, not 'close to the step', so it barely changes the distance the mechanism names. If RL's edge came from a final check against the problem's conditions, an RL finisher on a wrong base prefix cut at 75 % should still catch the error. It does not: 'Wrong base prefixes (n=70): RL finisher minus base finisher ... +5.7 [-2.9, 14.3]' at 75 % ('37/32/21 vs 25/20/17'). The item states: "Refuted: 'late checking' (no RL edge at 75 %)" and "RL's advantage is in the first half of the answer and is in the text by the halfway point". (2) result-855858: RL's check events fix errors no more often than the base's: 'blind judges call 5 of 80 check events a fix (base 3 of 40, RL 2 of 40'. What does differ is error production: 'first wrong steps per 1k finished tokens, 0.015 RL vs 0.038 base'. (3) result-96e819: when RL itself reviews its own finished drafts, it catches nothing: 'RL 454 (-0.6 [-1.4, 0.0], 0 fixed of 35 wrong / 3 broken)'. An RL that catches misreads by substituting into the conditions should fix some of its 35 wrong drafts when asked to check them. (4) result-faf15a puts the misread and slip difference at the moment the step is written, not at a later catch: 'Math-RL is about half as likely as the base to write the base's own located wrong step', and 'By label for Math 3.1: misread -1.52, slip -0.72, wrong plan +0.03: RL lowers misreadings and slips, not wrong plans.' Taken together, RL's lower misread and slip rate is prevention early in the answer. It is not a catch at the end, which is the part of m06 that does the explaining.

r7-m10.abandon: The board already measures RL's failure rate on the problems the base solves reliably, and it is far too low for a fixed set of persistent RL losses. (1) result-afc423 classes each held-out base sample by the base's other three samples and reports "in the class 'other three right' the base fails 7.2%, RL 0.9%". The mechanism says RL misses about a dozen base-reliable problems (the 12 base-only problems of result-5e17a6) in most of its own samples. In a class of roughly 1,500 problem-sample cells (base 1,642 of 2,000 right), 12 problems lost in 3 or more of RL's 4 samples would give at least 36 RL failures, about 2.4 % or more. The board measures 0.9 %, which leaves room for about 3 to 5 such problems at most. (2) result-e41d94 splits the 500 problems by fitted difficulty: "0.11 on the easiest 335 (base wrong cells 157/130/71, RL 117/35/8". On the easiest 335 problems, which is where problems the base solves reliably fall, RL has only 8 wrong cells in total. That cannot hold a dozen problems that RL misses in most samples. (3) result-9b6af3 shows that RL's single-sample losses are smaller than the base's own resampling losses ("loses 35 of its 410 right" for a fresh base-like sample against "RL plain fixes 65 and loses 12"). So RL's 12 base-only problems fit RL's own per-sample slip rate, with no excess left for a systematic loss. (4) result-5da8a9 finds a single difficulty axis, with cross-arm excess union "the same as two samples of one arm". The base-only cell is therefore a resampling draw, not a property of the RL arm. The mechanism's own first test (RL's mean right count of 4 on the base-only problems below 2.0) is already answered by (1) and (2): RL's per-sample failure rate on base-reliable problems is about 1 %, so its mean on those problems will be near 4 of 4, not below 2.
